Lane Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH AI adoption in Europe Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy San Francisco, 30 October 2026 My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy.[1 ] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy.[2 ] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system. I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system.[3 ] [4 ] Aggregate trends Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). While digital investment has grown far more quickly in the United States, the surge in digital investment (with an estimated clear acceleration since 2024) marks a distinct shift in the structure of the euro area economy.[5 ] As shown in Chart 1b, in the euro area digital investment has primarily been in intangible assets, while investment in data centres has constituted a relatively small share.[6 ] Chart 1 Digital investment in the euro area a) Digital investment proxy, euro area b) Digital investment proxy, euro area, with asset breakdown (2014 = 100) (EUR billion) Sources: Eurostat, ECB and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 1a shows the digital proxy for the euro area business economy, at constant 2020 prices, indexed to 2014. The blue dots for 2025 and 2026 extend the digital investment proxy based on the annual growth of an output proxy for digital services (weighted non-seasonally adjusted production of publishing activities; computer programming, consultancy and related activities; and information service activities). Chart 1b shows a digital proxy which refers to (i) investment in non-residential buildings and structures in the information and communication sector, (ii) information and communication technology (ICT) equipment in the business economy, (iii) investment in computer software and databases (CSDBs) in the business economy, excluding the ICT sector, and (iv) total intellectual property products (IPP) investment (in CSDBs and research and development) by the ICT sector. Missing country values are estimated based on known euro area aggregates of country-sector shares. On a whole-economy basis, digital investment has increased from around 2.3 per cent of euro area GDP in 2014 to 3.0 per cent in 2024 (and looks to have increased to 3.3 per cent by the end of the first half of 2026, on the basis of updates of digital services output). The latest observations are for 2024 for euro area annual accounts and July 2026 for euro area production data. In the ECB Corporate Telephone Survey, firms report that AI has added about 10 per cent to their capital expenditure plans this year. AI-related demand has helped activity to hold up over the last two years – as reflected by the contributions of the “computers and other electronics” and “information and communication services” sectors to total market production (Chart 2a). As illustrated in Chart 2b, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicators show that output, employment and new orders have developed considerably more favourably in the technology equipment subsector than in other manufacturing subsectors. For services, the software subsector has performed better than other services sectors in terms of output, albeit not in terms of employment and new orders. Sources: S&P Global and ECB calculations. Notes: Sectoral labels are taken from the July Global PMI press release. The latest observations are for September 2026. AI has been the main driver of global goods trade over the last year (Chart 3a). European firms are contributors to the global AI supply chain. Table 4 shows that AI-related exports and imports are growing quickly in the euro area, especially in relation to core data centre goods, which contain directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage and networking capacity. Possibly related to differences in composition, the increase in AI import prices in the euro area is more muted than for the other major economic regions (Chart 3b). Chart 5 shows that, while AI-related price increases have contributed materially to the upward shift in goods inflation, the impact on headline inflation is limited owing to the relatively low weight of AI-exposed goods in the consumer price index (13.3 per cent in the non-energy industrial goods subcomponent and 3.4 per cent of the HICP). AI intensity groups are based on OECD methodology (for details, see “A sectoral taxonomy of AI intensity ”, OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers , No 30, December 2024). The classification comprises three AI intensity groups: high, medium and low, based on sectoral quartile allocations across four indicators: 1. AI human capital; 2. AI innovation; 3. Barrier-adjusted AI exposure; and 4. AI use. A sector is classified as high if it ranks in the top quartile for at least two indicators and not in the bottom quartile for the remaining two, and as low if it ranks in the bottom quartile for at least two indicators and not in the top quartile for the remaining two. Sectors such as IT services, media, telecommunications, finance and scientific research and development are classified as high-intensity, while food products, textiles, wood and paper, construction and hospitality are low-intensity. Sectors falling outside these criteria are classified as medium AI-intensive. The latest observations are for 20 October 2026. US firms (especially the hyperscalers building out the AI infrastructure) have been large-scale issuers of euro-denominated bonds (reverse Yankees). So far, the available data show that purchases by European investors of euro-denominated bonds issued by US firms have increased alongside a decline in their purchases of US Treasury bonds (Chart 9a).[8 ] The AI boom has also led to large initial public offerings (IPOs), including the SpaceX IPO in the second quarter of 2026. In this context, euro area investors have stepped up their acquisitions of US equities, and at the same time they have lowered their purchases of other foreign equities (Chart 9b). Overall, these developments, together with analysis of credit spreads and the book-cover ratios of euro area corporate issuers and credit spreads, suggest only limited crowding-out up to now.[9 ] Chart 9 Absorption of US AI issuance in the euro area a) Issuance and absorption of reverse Yankees b) US IPOs and euro area purchases of foreign equities (average of quarterly flows in EUR billions) (average of quarterly flows in EUR billions) Source: ECB SHSS (Securities Holdings Statistics by Sector). The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Finally, lending to AI-related firms has contributed substantially to aggregate credit growth. This is evident in Chart 10, which shows that the ECB Broad Intermediate Gauge (ECB-BIG) index would have indicated a tighter credit environment in the absence of AI-related lending. In response to a dedicated question in the October 2026 bank lending survey on the significance and impact of AI adoption, several banks indicated that they expect a gradual but sustained increase in loan demand to finance digital infrastructure, particularly data centres. Banks also reported that their current and prospective AI-related lending is more likely to target infrastructure providers rather than software developers or firms adopting AI, with this focus expected to become more pronounced over the coming months. I will now turn from aggregate trends to firm-level and household-level surveys on AI adoption before examining how AI is being funded by the financial system. AI adoption The pace of AI adoption by European firms has trended upwards since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. Chart 11 shows that the proportion of firms citing AI-related topics in earnings calls has expanded from about 10 per cent to about 40 per cent over this period. A similar pattern is evident in our Corporate Telephone Survey. Chart 11 Alternative measures of AI adoption Proportion of firms mentioning AI or related terms (percentage of firms) Sources: NL Analytics, Corporate Telephone Survey Team and ECB calculations. Notes: CTS (Corporate Telephone Survey) refers to the proportion of euro area firms which mentioned “AI” during the call; Earnings calls refer to the quarterly average proportion of euro area firms which mentioned “AI”, “artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “large language models”, “LLM”, or alternatives during the earnings call. The dashed lines indicate the trend since the second quarter of 2023. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. The earnings calls data show significant variation across sectors.[10 ] The left panel of Chart 12 shows that there has been an increase in the range of sectors in which firms frame AI as an innovation that expands the technology frontier. Although less widespread, there has also been an increase in the range of sectors in which AI is seen as potentially reducing costs by improving production efficiency (right panel). While the earnings calls data cover publicly listed firms, our Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) is a large-scale survey that covers both large firms and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).[11 ] In the fourth quarter of 2025 most firms participating in the SAFE reported that they were using AI: 64 per cent of firms said they were using it either experimentally or moderately, while only 7 per cent of firms reported that their use was “significant” (Chart 13).[12 ] In terms of the reasons to use AI, 62 per cent cited improving business processes and 23 per cent cited innovation, research and development or expanding their range of products, while just 15 per cent cited reducing labour costs. The latest observations are for the fourth quarter of 2025. The round of the SAFE survey conducted in the fourth quarter of 2025 also ran a field experiment to test whether planned AI investment by a firm responds to perceived competitive pressure from domestic peer firms and foreign peer firms.[13 ] Chart 14a shows that firms underestimate the rate of AI adoption by their peer firms, with most firms underestimating the share of competitors that have invested in AI, some by as much as 50 percentage points. The results of the field experiment indicate that providing information about the AI investment plans of their peers makes firms change their beliefs. In the field experiment, half of the firms were randomly told the true share of peers investing in AI, at home and abroad. These firms revised up their beliefs about the share of peers investing in AI, by 4.3 percentage points for domestic competitors and 3.3 percentage points for foreign competitors. Chart 14b shows a striking asymmetry: firms plan more AI investment when they expect more domestic peers to invest, whereas beliefs about the AI investment plans of foreign firms have no effect. The impact of domestic competition is sizeable: a 1 percentage point increase in the expected share of domestic firms undertaking AI investment raises their own expected AI investment rate by about 0.6 percentage points. That is a marked increase, given an average expected AI investment rate of 8.3 per cent. According to the round of the SAFE survey conducted in the second quarter of 2026, among firms planning AI-related investment over the next twelve months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training. Firms were allowed to indicate multiple types of expected AI-related investment: 49 per cent plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure, and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. Investment patterns are broadly similar across firm sizes, although the shares are consistently higher for large firms than for SMEs across all investment types. Turning to AI adoption by workers, our Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) asks households on a regular basis about AI usage in the workplace. According to the CES, the proportion of workers using AI has doubled over the last two years, with 52 per cent now reporting that they use AI at work, compared with 26 per cent in 2024 (Chart 16a).[14 ] Adoption rates are higher for younger and more educated workers (Chart 16b).[15 ] Chart 16 AI adoption rates in the euro area a) AI adoption rates among workers, 2024-2026 b) AI adoption rates by demographic groups, 2026 (percentage of respondents) (percentage of respondents) Sources: CES (Consumer Expectations Survey) and ECB calculations based on the earning calls database.Notes: The chart shows the share of employed workers reporting the use of AI in their work. The question reads: “Do you personally use artificial intelligence (including a large language model, such as ChatGPT or Gemini) in your work?” Chart 17a reports the time saved by workers on a range of tasks. The median working user reports saving three hours per week, or about 7.7 per cent of median working time.[16 ] However, the distribution is highly skewed: most users enjoy only moderate time savings, while a small number report very high efficiency gains. Generating or debugging code yields the largest gains, at six hours per week, although only around 15 per cent of workers use AI for this purpose. A similar pattern emerges for data analysis, automation of routine tasks and creating audio or visual content. By contrast, research, information gathering, writing and text editing are among the most frequently cited uses. Yet time savings reported for these tasks are considerably lower than for more technical tasks such as coding. In most professions, workers do not see perceived efficiency gains as a threat to their jobs (Chart 17b). The occupations that have the highest adoption rates tend to save the most hours and have more positive views of AI. For example, managers use AI the most, save the most time and ultimately have the most positive perception of the technology; this places them in a good position to help steer AI adoption in the workplace.[17 ] Chart 17 AI at the workplace and hours saved a) Tasks performed with AI and hours saved per week b) Hours saved, adoption and sentiment about AI across occupations (upper scale: percentage of workers using AI; lower scale: median number of hours per week) (x-axis: percentage of workers; y-axis: number of hours saved per week) Source: Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann D. Time saved per task represents the average total weekly hours saved by workers who reported using AI for that specific activity. Respondents can select multiple tasks, and those who reported saving significant time with AI are more likely to choose a greater number of tasks, which mechanically inflates the average hours saved. A comparison of the AI financing plans of firms within the same country, industry and size class indicates that more tangible investment tilts financing towards external sources (Chart 23). The use of external finance for AI appears to hinge on the tangibility of the underlying investment: assets that are pledgeable or collateralisable attract external funding, whereas more intangible expenditures are financed internally. In contrast, employee training represents a smaller, more incremental and intangible expense that firms can more readily finance out of retained earnings. Conclusions This speech has highlighted that AI is currently a significant contributor to growth in the euro area, driven by both expenditure on AI adoption and the role of European firms in the global AI supply chain. Surveys of firms and households indicate significant AI adoption rates, albeit unevenly distributed across sectors and demographic groups. A striking pattern is that European households are net positive about the employment impact of AI. However, the AI adoption process is still at a relatively early stage and the extent and timing of the economy-wide transformative potential of AI remain highly uncertain. The European financial system has responded to the external financing needs generated by increased AI activity, even if internal funding remains the most important source of funding. European investors are also major investors in foreign AI equities and the euro-denominated bond issuances by American hyperscalers, even if the latter are primarily funded by a lower allocation to US Treasury bonds. Looking ahead, tracking the near-term and medium-term implications of AI will remain high on the analytical agenda at the ECB. The Board of Directors acknowledged his request at its meeting held on 29 October 2026. Mr Ioan Nani has led the company for nearly three decades, transforming a traditional manufacturing business into a benchmark for stability and performance in the Romanian pharmaceutical industry. After a professional life devoted almost entirely to the company, his wish to spend more time with his family and loved ones is entirely natural. Under his leadership, Antibiotice has become one of Romania’s leading generic pharmaceutical manufacturers, with a portfolio spanning prescription medicines (Rx) and non-Rx products, including over-the-counter medicines, food supplements and medical devices. The company exports its products to 70 countries and holds a position as a world leader in the production of the active pharmaceutical ingredient nystatin. Beyond these figures, Antibiotice remains a strong and respected brand, supported by a highly skilled team, processes certified to international standards and an outstanding reputation in an industry with quality requirements as stringent as those of the pharmaceutical sector. Until 4 December 2026, Mr Ioan Nani will continue to exercise his duties in full and, together with the Board of Directors, oversee the transition process. The company’s activities will continue in accordance with the Administration Plan approved by shareholders. The executive team under his leadership will ensure the continuity of day-to-day operations, relationships with partners in Romania and international markets, and ongoing investment projects. For the period following 4 December 2026, the Board of Directors will appoint an interim Chief Executive Officer and conduct the selection process for a new Chief Executive Officer in accordance with Government Emergency Ordinance No. 109/2011 on the corporate governance of public enterprises. Each decision adopted in this respect will be disclosed to the capital market through a current report. The company’s strategic objectives remain unchanged: sustainable business development, strengthening its position in the domestic market, expanding its international presence and safeguarding shareholders’ long-term interests. The Board of Directors, executive management and employees of Antibiotice express their sincere gratitude to Mr Ioan Nani for everything he has built and for leaving the company strong and ready for its next chapter. Here at Antibiotice, he is—and always will be—at home. President of the Management Board, Ionuț-Sebastian IAVOR
